newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas trade meet faces north-south divide.
newsitem.headline: Americas trade meet faces north-south divide.

text.p: Ministers from 34 nations in the Americas started a meeting in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte on Friday facing a north-south divide on how to spread free trade throughout the region.

Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia, presiding over the opening session, reaffirmed his country's desire to advance with caution and care in setting up the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
"We are not engaged here in some exercise of rhetoric that will lead us to a declaration of principles of a merely symbolic or exhortative value," Lampreia said.
"We are engaged in what might very well prove to be the greatest initiative of commercial diplomacy of the majority of our countries in the coming years," he said.
The FTAA was launched at the Miami summit in 1994 and envisaged a free trade zone stretching from the Bering Strait to the plains of Patagonia after the year 2005.
With a combined gross domestic product in excess of $9.0 trillion and almost one billion consumers, the FTAA would be the biggest free trade area in the world.
Lower-level talks this week in Belo Horizonte to prepare for Friday's ministerial get-together failed to reach consensus on how to launch formal trade negotiations, officials said.
All would like to start the talks after a presidential FTAA summit in Chile next March.
But South America's Mercosur trade bloc of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay wants to proceed with care, negotiating in stages, with tariff cuts left until last.
The United States, on the other hand, is pushing for speed, and wants to discuss everything from tariff reductions to subsidies at the same time.
"What is going on is a war of equilibrium (between the United States and Mercosur)," said Stefan Bogdan Salej, president of the Minas Gerais industry federation FIEMG.

Salej said the struggle for influence between Washington and Brasilia, which is acting as spokesman for its Mercosur partners, partly reflected a growing awareness in South America of the importance of trade with the European Union.
"American business still treats us in a neo-colonialist way. The Europeans treat us differently," he told Reuters.
In debating a draft ministerial declaration, made available to Reuters, the ministers will have to decide whether they "will" or "should" launch formal talks next March.

The ministers will also have to decide whether to allow the labour movement a greater advisory role in the negotiating process. Business leaders already hold official parallel forums to FTAA meetings.
Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso warned on Thursday night that the FTAA would only be possible if it brought clear social benefits.

Foreign Minister Lampreia on Friday distributed to his counterparts a "Manifesto of the Workers of the Americas," drafted earlier in the week by trade unionists meeting in Belo Horizonte and which demands worker's rights be safeguarded.
